p: The wheel is commonly spoken of as the first of all inventions, the very emblem of human ingenuity, and the phrase reinventing the wheel is used in our offices to reproach a clerk for wasting his time. It may therefore surprise you to learn that the wheel is a comparatively late invention, younger than farming by several thousand years, younger than pottery, younger than towns, and that some great civilisations did very well without it.

The Encyclopaedia of the future tells me that the earliest evidence of wheeled vehicles appears, quite suddenly and over a wide area, about five thousand five hundred years ago, between roughly three thousand six hundred and three thousand four hundred years before Christ. There are pictures of wagons on clay tablets from Uruk, in Mesopotamia; there is a pot from a place called Bronocice in Poland painted with what seems to be a four-wheeled wagon; and there is an actual wooden wheel, with its axle, found preserved in a marsh near Ljubljana, in the Austrian province of Carniola, which is thought to be more than five thousand years old. Which people first made it is unknown. It spread so quickly across Europe and the Near East that it is difficult to say where it began.

The potter's wheel, it should be said, is older than the wagon wheel, or at least as old; in Mesopotamia the slow turning-table on which pots were shaped was in use before carts were known. Some scholars think that the wheel for pots suggested the wheel for carts. Others doubt it. A wheel that turns on a fixed spindle in a workshop and a wheel that carries a load across rough ground are very different problems.
## Why it is harder than it looks

The difficulty is not the wheel. Any child who has rolled a log knows that round things roll. The difficulty is the axle: the joint between the wheel and the cart. If the axle is too tight, it will not turn; if too loose, it wobbles and breaks. The hole in the wheel must be almost perfectly round and smooth, and the end of the axle the same, and they must fit closely together, and both must be strong enough to bear the weight. This required good tools of metal, of which copper had only lately come into use, and skilled carpentry. The earliest wheels were solid discs of wood, often made of three planks joined together, heavy and slow, and the earliest wagons were drawn by oxen, at the pace of a walking man.

The swift spoked wheel, light and strong, with a rim supported by thin rods radiating from the hub, appeared about four thousand years ago, among the peoples of the steppes east of the Ural mountains, whose graves have been found with the remains of chariots in them. A chariot drawn by two horses, carrying a driver and an archer, was the most terrible weapon of the ancient world for many centuries. It carried the conquerors of the second millennium before Christ into India, into Egypt, into China and into Greece. The heroes of Homer fight from chariots, though Homer, writing much later, seems not quite to have understood how they were used, and has his heroes drive to the battle and then get down and fight on foot, like gentlemen alighting from a cab.

The peoples of the Americas, before the coming of the Spaniards, did not use the wheel for transport, though in Mexico they made little wheeled figures of animals, apparently as toys or ornaments. This is not because they were less clever. The great civilisations of Mexico and Peru built cities, temples, roads and calendars of extraordinary refinement. But they had no horses, oxen or other large animals that could be harnessed to a cart; the llama of the Andes will carry a modest load upon its back and refuses, with great dignity, to do anything more. Without a beast to pull it, a cart is of little use, and on the steep mountain roads of the Incas a wheel would have been worse than useless.

Even in the Old World the wheel was not universally preferred. In the Near East and North Africa, in the centuries after the Romans, the camel largely replaced the cart, because a camel needs no road, and roads are expensive. A traveller in the Arab lands in the Middle Ages might go his whole life without seeing a wheeled vehicle. The wheel, then, is not a simple advance that every people adopts once it is known. It is a tool that suits certain conditions: flat land, made roads, and strong animals to draw it.

Where those conditions held, the wheel became the foundation of commerce and of war. It turned the potter's clay, and later the miller's stone, driven by water and by wind. It became the spinning wheel, the cogwheel, the pulley and the flywheel. Every engine of my own century is a congregation of wheels, from the paddle steamer to the locomotive, which is nothing but a fire set upon wheels and made to pull more wheels behind it. And the men of the future tell me that it is wheels again, driven by engines of a new kind, that carry them, at speeds that would kill an Englishman of my generation with fright, along roads of a smoothness that would astonish the Romans.
